nameStory: This tiny fungus gets its peculiar name from its resemblance to a miniature tuning fork, but not in the way you might expect! The 'tuning fork' actually refers to the microscopic structures that produce its spores, which split into two prongs just like the musical instrument.
description: The club-like tuning fork is a small jelly fungus that looks like tiny yellow fingers poking up from rotting wood. These slender, tapering growths are somewhat rubbery and translucent, resembling miniature coral or small yellow candles. Individual specimens are quite small, reaching only about an inch tall and just a few millimeters wide. Despite their delicate appearance, they have a distinctly gelatinous, bouncy texture when fresh.

idTips.label: Yellow finger-like shape
idTips.description: Small, bright yellow growths that taper to a point like tiny fingers or clubs, often growing in small clusters

idTips.label: Jelly-like texture
idTips.description: Feels rubbery and bouncy when gently pressed, like a firm gelatin dessert that springs back to shape

idTips.label: Growing on dead wood
idTips.description: Always found on decaying logs, branches, or woody debris, never on living trees or soil

idTips.label: Translucent appearance
idTips.description: Semi-transparent when held up to light, with a waxy or plastic-like shine when dry

idTips.label: Small clustered growth
idTips.description: Individual specimens are pencil-eraser sized or smaller, often appearing in small groups of 3-10

habitat: Look for this fungus on decaying hardwood logs and branches in moist deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England. It's particularly common on well-rotted wood that's been decomposing for several seasons, often in shaded areas where moisture lingers. You'll find it from sea level to moderate elevations, especially in areas with consistent humidity like stream valleys or dense woodlands.

seasonality.spring: Fresh specimens begin appearing as temperatures warm and moisture increases, often found on winter-weathered logs. This is an excellent time to spot bright yellow, fully hydrated specimens.
seasonality.summer: Active growth continues in humid conditions, though specimens may shrivel during dry spells and plump back up after rain. Look for them after summer thunderstorms.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for observation as autumn rains rehydrate specimens and new flushes appear. The yellow color contrasts nicely with fallen leaves, making identification easier.
seasonality.winter: Specimens become shriveled and darker, appearing almost orange or brown, but will rehydrate during winter thaws. They're harder to spot but still present on protected logs.

funFact: This fungus can completely shrivel up into tiny, hard, unrecognizable bumps during dry weather, then magically plump back up into its full jelly-finger glory within hours of getting wet again - like nature's own sponge animal toys!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with its larger cousin, the jelly-antler fungus, but club-like tuning fork specimens are much smaller (under an inch) and simpler in shape. Remember: if it's bigger than your thumb or has branching antler-like growth, it's probably the jelly-antler instead.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'jelly fungus,' this species belongs to a completely different group than the more familiar wood ear or other common jelly fungi. The Dacrymycetaceae family represents an ancient lineage of fungi with unique spore-producing structures that scientists use to classify them.
compareHints: The club-like tuning fork is much smaller and simpler than its relative the jelly-antler, which grows larger and develops branched, antler-like projections. While jelly-antler can reach several inches and has multiple branches, club-like tuning fork stays small and finger-like. Both have the same rubbery texture and bright yellow color when fresh, but size and branching pattern are reliable distinguishing features.
